messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 44
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nurse
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Hopelessness: I have no future

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ravi is a 44-year-old Filipino American man who has worked for years as a nurse, the kind of person his family had long relied on for steadiness, practical judgment, and patience. He is married and had been used to moving through long hospital shifts with a clear sense of purpose. That changed after he was mugged while walking back to his car after an evening shift. The parking structure was dim and mostly empty, and he remembered noticing footsteps that seemed to echo behind him before he reached his vehicle. When he turned, a man closed the distance quickly, demanded his wallet, and struck him when he hesitated. Ravi remembered the event not as a flowing sequence but as stark visual fragments: the shine of concrete under fluorescent light, the attacker’s hand, the angle of the man’s face, the hard ground rushing up. He was hit and hurt in the struggle, and what stayed with him afterward was not only fear but the bodily memory of where he had been injured. When the memory came back, he felt pain again in those same places, as if his body were replaying the assault along with the images.

In the weeks that followed, Ravi found that the mugging lived in his mind as pictures rather than a story. He would say it was like looking at photographs: disconnected but vivid, frozen images that arrived without warning. A glimpse of a shadow in a reflective surface, the sense of footsteps behind him, or entering a parking lot at the end of a shift could bring back the same visual frames. At those moments he did not simply remember what had happened; he felt it in his body, with a painful echo of the blows he had taken. What frightened him most was how quickly ordinary moments could become charged. Passing a mirrored wall at the hospital, he would catch himself checking it repeatedly, using the reflection to make sure no one was coming up behind him. If he walked down a corridor or through the staff garage, he kept looking over his shoulder, certain that failing to do so would leave him exposed.

Ravi’s days became organized around trying to stay ahead of danger. He scanned entrances, corners, and parking areas automatically, searching other people’s posture and movements for signs of threat. In the cafeteria, in meetings, even at family restaurants, he chose his seat based on where he could see the door and protect his back. At work, this meant he stopped sitting where colleagues usually gathered during breaks and instead positioned himself at the edge of the room, where he could watch who came in and out. Coworkers noticed he seemed distracted or tense, though Ravi did not know how to explain that he felt he had to keep checking. Mirrors became part of the same routine. He looked into them not out of vanity but because they offered another angle on the space around him, a way to monitor what might be behind him.

When he was not watching his surroundings, he worked hard to keep his mind occupied. He filled silence with tasks, extra charting, television in the background, phone games, anything that might prevent the images from surfacing. At home, his wife saw him move from one activity to another without settling. If there was nothing immediate to do, the stillness became intolerable. Nights were the hardest. He had trouble falling asleep, and when he did sleep, he woke easily, alert and listening. Bed no longer felt like a place where he could let down his guard. Fatigue followed him into his shifts, and he found himself relying even more on routines of checking and mental busyness just to get through the day.

Alongside this, Ravi had come to believe something about the attack said something fundamental about him. He was certain there was something about him that made it happen, as if he had carried some weakness that others could detect. He did not describe this as a passing thought but as a conclusion that had settled heavily into his view of himself. From there, his sense of the future narrowed. He told himself that nothing good could happen anymore, that whatever life he had before was over, and at times he felt with bleak certainty that he had no future at all. These beliefs sat beside the practical facts of his life—his marriage, his job, his responsibilities—but did not loosen in the face of them.

By the time he sought help, the strain was showing across home and work. His wife had begun asking why he was always on edge and why even simple outings required so much planning about where to sit and how to leave. At the hospital, he was still functioning, but each shift felt like an exercise in vigilance rather than care. What finally brought him in was not a single new crisis but the realization that he could no longer imagine continuing like this: sleeping poorly, policing every environment, filling every spare second so the images would not return. He came to treatment wanting relief from the constant sense of danger, but also with a quieter hope he could barely trust—that he might one day walk to his car, sit in a room, or lie down beside his wife without feeling that he had to be on guard.
